blue.definition: The blue bin is for plastic packaging: the bottles, jugs, tubs and trays most homes throw away every day. A sorting plant separates plastic by type later, so your part is simple. Keep it empty, rinsed and apart from everything else.
accepts: Water, juice and soft-drink bottles
Bottles of shampoo, detergent and cleaning liquid
Yogurt tubs, margarine tubs and food trays
Plastic jugs and containers marked with a recycling number from 1 to 7
Clean plastic caps, screwed back onto the bottle
rejects: Plastic bags and wrapping film, which need a separate drop-off point
Containers that held motor oil, paint or pesticides (they belong in the red bin)
Food-soiled plastic you cannot rinse clean
Number 3 (PVC) and number 6 (PS, foam) plastics are often refused by local collectors, so check first
prepare: Empty it completely
Rinse with a little water; there is no need to scrub
Squeeze out the air and put the cap back on, so more fits in the bin
Leave the label on; the plant removes it
blue.why: Plastic that is clean and sorted can become new containers, fibers and pipes. A greasy tub can spoil the clean plastic around it, so a quick rinse makes a real difference.

yellow.definition: The yellow bin takes paper-based packaging and printed paper. Its one rule is to stay dry and clean, because paper fibers are only worth recycling while they are in good condition.
accepts: Newspapers, magazines, office paper and envelopes
Cardboard boxes, flattened
Egg cartons and paper bags
Milk and juice cartons, rinsed and flattened
Notebooks and paperback books, with plastic covers removed
rejects: Greasy or food-stained paper, such as the bottom of a pizza box
Used tissues, napkins and paper towels
Wet, moldy or burnt paper
Paper coated with plastic or foil, such as many snack wrappers
prepare: Keep it dry until collection
Flatten boxes and cartons to save space
Pull off large pieces of tape and plastic windows
Rinse cartons and let them drain
yellow.why: Wet or greasy paper is hard to recycle and can spoil the clean paper around it. Keeping paper dry is the single most useful habit for this bin.

green.definition: The green bin is for glass packaging only. Bottle and jar glass can be melted and made into new glass again and again without losing quality, as long as it is not mixed with other materials.
accepts: Drink bottles of any color
Food jars: sauce, jam, pickles and spreads
Perfume and cosmetic bottles, once empty
Clean medicine bottles with no liquid left inside
rejects: Ceramics, porcelain, cups and plates
Mirrors and window glass
Light bulbs and tubes (take them to a special collection point)
Heat-resistant glass such as oven dishes, which melts at a different temperature
prepare: Empty it and give it a quick rinse
Remove lids; metal lids go in the grey bin
Labels can stay on
Wrap broken glass in thick paper and mark the package, so collectors are not hurt
green.why: One piece of ceramic or oven glass can cause defects in a whole batch of new glass. Keeping the bin pure is what makes glass recycling work.

grey.definition: The grey bin holds metal packaging and small metal items. Metal is valuable: it can be recycled many times, and making it from recycled material takes far less energy than making it from ore.
accepts: Aluminum drink cans
Steel food tins
Clean aluminum foil and trays
Metal jar lids and bottle caps
Small scrap such as old pots and cutlery
rejects: Cans that held paint or chemicals (red bin)
Aerosol cans that still contain product
Batteries and electronics (special collection)
Large scrap such as pipes, appliances and car parts; sell or give these to a scrap collector
prepare: Empty and rinse it
Press sharp lid edges inward
Scrunch foil into a ball so it does not blow away
Keep metal away from food waste
grey.why: Aluminum saves the most energy when recycled, and scrap metal also has market value, so collectors in many areas will take it from you.

brown.tagline: Food scraps, garden waste and clean wood
brown.definition: The brown bin is for material that was once alive and can rot back into soil. Composted properly, it becomes a natural soil improver instead of a pile of smelly waste.
accepts: Fruit and vegetable peels and leftovers
Coffee grounds, tea bags and eggshells
Leaves, grass clippings and small branches
Untreated wood offcuts and sawdust
rejects: Plastic and plastic bags, including ones labeled as biodegradable
Cooking oil and large amounts of grease
Pet waste and diapers (black bin)
Painted, varnished or treated wood (special collection)
prepare: Drain off liquid before it goes in
Wrap scraps in paper, never in a plastic bag
Cut branches into short pieces
Keep a lid on the kitchen container to limit smells and flies
brown.why: Food buried in a landfill rots without air and gives off methane, a strong greenhouse gas. Sent to compost, the same scraps feed the soil.

special.tagline: Electronics, batteries, textiles and building waste
special.definition: This is not a bin you fill at home. It stands for items that need a collection point or a pickup of their own, because they hold valuable parts, or because they do not belong in ordinary waste at all.
accepts: Phones, chargers, cables and other small electronics
Large appliances such as TVs, fridges and washing machines
Batteries of every kind
Clothes, shoes and fabric; give wearable items away first
Rubble, tiles and plasterboard from building work
rejects: Ordinary household waste
Liquids such as paint and solvents (red bin)
Anything that is simply broken but still useful: repair or donate it first
prepare: Tape the terminals of batteries with insulating tape
Do not open, crush or burn devices or batteries
Delete your personal data from phones and computers
Arrange a pickup for large items instead of leaving them on the street
special.why: Electronics and batteries contain metals worth recovering and substances that must not reach soil or water. A damaged battery can also start a fire inside a waste truck.

red.definition: The red bin is a warning color. It is for items that can poison, burn or injure people, animals or water supplies. They need special handling and a proper collection point. Never pour them down the drain.
accepts: Paint, thinners, solvents and pesticides
Used motor oil and strong cleaning chemicals
Expired or unused medicines, returned to a pharmacy
Needles and blades in a rigid, closed container
Used masks and gloves, sealed in a bag
rejects: Ordinary household waste
Chemicals mixed together in one container
Loose needles in a bag
Anything poured down a sink, toilet or into the soil
prepare: Keep chemicals in their original container with the label on
Never mix different products
Close caps tightly and store upright, away from heat and children
Use a thick plastic bottle with a lid as a sharps container, and mark it clearly
red.why: A small amount of chemical or medicine can contaminate a lot of water, and loose sharps injure the people who handle waste. When in doubt, check with your local authorities.

black.tagline: Everything that cannot go anywhere else
black.definition: The black bin is the last option. It takes ordinary waste that cannot be recycled, composted or collected separately, and it ends up in landfill. Before you use it, ask once: can this be reused, recycled or composted?
accepts: Used tissues, napkins and hygiene products
Diapers and sealed pet waste
Broken ceramics, cups and plates
Greasy or soiled paper and food wrappers
Dust, sweepings and cooled ashes
rejects: Anything recyclable: check the other bins first
Batteries and electronics (special collection)
Chemicals, medicines and sharps (red bin)
Hot ashes or embers
prepare: Bag it and tie the bag tightly
Let ashes cool completely
Do not overfill, so the bag can be carried without tearing
Sort the rest of your waste first; this bin should be the smallest
black.why: Everything in this bin ends in landfill, so each item you send to another bin makes the pile smaller.
